extracted.intended_audience: NPR listeners and general public interested in biomedical research, science journalists, and policy-interested readers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical considerations for judging the quality, reliability, and ethical readiness of biomedical and preclinical research (especially animal studies) as discussed in a journalistic interview about reproducibility and perverse incentives. Useful for reviewers, journalists, and policy analysts assessing research claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies should be reproducible; many published findings fail replication (example: of 53 promising studies Amgen tried to reproduce, only six could be reproduced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replication attempts — even with help from original scientists — are a key test of credibility. Treat a single positive result cautiously until independently reproduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate sample size / statistical power
rubrics_metrics.description: Using very few animals (e.g., too few mice) can lead to mistaken conclusions and non-reproducible results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments with sufficient numbers to detect real effects and avoid overinterpreting small-sample findings; reviewers should flag underpowered studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of biological variables (e.g., genetics of model organisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers must take into account genetics and other biological characteristics of animal models; failure to do so undermines validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether studies controlled for or reported strain, sex, genetic background, and other variables that can affect outcomes in preclinical models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful laboratory practices and error avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical mistakes in the lab (handling, protocols, measurement errors) can produce false or irreproducible findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether methods are described in sufficient detail, whether standard operating procedures and quality controls were used, and whether staff had appropriate training/oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and openness to assist replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharing methods and cooperating with replicators is important; original researchers sometimes help, but openness alone may not guarantee reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for clear methods, available data/protocols, and willingness to share materials; absence of such transparency is a red flag for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding perverse incentives (publish-or-perish effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitive pressures to publish quickly, secure grants, and obtain tenure can prompt cutting corners and lower scientific rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether incentives (career, funding) may have biased study design, analysis, or reporting; systemic pressures should be accounted for when evaluating research reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research motivation: focus on truth/delight vs. career/financial goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Research driven by curiosity and pursuit of truth ('delight') is more likely to be careful and reliable than work driven primarily by career or financial incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the research agenda and framing suggest genuine hypothesis-driven inquiry versus chasing trendy, high-impact outputs for career advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward single-study claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual studies are often contingent and may not stand the test of time; readers and journalists should question single-study claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overhyping single studies in reporting or practice change; require corroboration from multiple independent studies before drawing strong conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism and external validity of preclinical models
rubrics_metrics.description: Preclinical studies must be realistic and relevant; many promising preclinical results fail to translate to effective human treatments (example: ALS drug studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate model validity, translational relevance, and how well experimental conditions mimic the clinical situation before endorsing clinical trials or clinical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication as an intentional quality-control practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate, systematic replication efforts (e.g., independent review of studies) can reveal widespread flaws and are critical to assessing what findings are reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support and value replication studies; treat successful independent replications as strong evidence and failed replications as signals to re-evaluate methods and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical readiness for human trials (evidence threshold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patients may enroll in experimental therapies based on flawed science; robust, reliable preclinical evidence is ethically required before human experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require strong, well-replicated preclinical data and clear risk/benefit justification before advancing to human trials; flag trials based on weak preclinical foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic factors: funding environment affects research quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Shrinking funds and proposed budget cuts (e.g., NIH) increase competition and intensify perverse incentives, potentially worsening overall research quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider policy and funding context as background when evaluating research ecosystems; resource constraints can explain and exacerbate methodological compromises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility about the literature's reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists and consumers of research should recognize that a substantial portion of the literature may be incorrect or contingent ('probably half of this is wrong').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt measured conclusions, prioritize replication and meta-analysis, and avoid definitive claims based on limited evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize thoroughness over speed to publish
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing quickly even if it means getting things wrong contributes to flawed science; thorough, careful work should be valued over rapid publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing or evaluating research, reward methodological rigor, completeness, and careful validation rather than novelty or speed alone.
